name: Ethiopian Doro Wat
description: Doro wat depends on a real technique found nowhere else: the onions are cooked completely dry, no oil at all, for a long stretch until they break down into a thick, caramelized paste - only then does the niter kibbeh, garlic, ginger, and real berbere go in. A hard-boiled egg simmered right in the sauce is a genuine, essential part of the dish, not a garnish to skip.
steps_detailed: Marinate the chicken in the lemon juice for 15-20 minutes.

Cook the onion alone in a dry pot, no oil, over medium-low heat, stirring often, 25-30 minutes, until it breaks down into a thick, deeply caramelized paste - this real dry-cook is the foundation of doro wat and cannot be rushed or skipped.
Add the ghee, garlic, and ginger, and cook 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the berbere and tomato paste, and cook 2 minutes more.
Add the chicken and a splash of water, and simmer 25-28 minutes until the chicken is very tender.
Add the whole hard-boiled egg in the last 10 minutes to soak up the sauce.

name: Ethiopian Injera
description: Injera, a spongy, slightly sour flatbread made from fermented teff, is the utensil, plate, and side all at once for Ethiopian meals - real injera ferments for two to three days, developing genuine sourness through wild fermentation, which this quicker version can only approximate.
steps_detailed: Whisk the teff flour, all-purpose flour, vinegar, and 1 cup water into a thin, smooth batter.
Let sit at room temperature at least 8 hours, ideally 24, to develop real tang.
Pour a thin layer into a hot, lightly oiled non-stick pan and cook, covered, without flipping, 2-3 minutes, until bubbles (the real 'eyes') cover the surface and the edges lift cleanly.

name: Ethiopian Misir Wat
description: Misir wat, red lentils simmered in a real berbere-spiced sauce, is one of Ethiopia's most essential everyday dishes, especially central during fasting periods when meat is set aside.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion in the oil over medium heat, stirring, 10-12 minutes, until deeply softened.
Add the garlic and berbere, and cook 1-2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the lentils and 1.5 cups water, and simmer 20-22 minutes until tender.
steps: Cook the onion in the oil over medium heat, stirring, 10-12 minutes, until deeply softened.

Add the lentils and 1.5 cups water, and simmer 20-22 minutes until tender.

name: Ethiopian Tibs
description: Tibs, sautéed cubes of meat with onion, pepper, and rosemary, is a beloved Ethiopian dish, real technique searing the meat hot and fast rather than stewing it, keeping the interior tender.
steps_detailed: Sear the beef in the ghee over high heat, 4-5 minutes, until well browned but still tender inside.
Add the onion, bell pepper, jalapeño, and garlic, and cook 5-6 minutes more.

name: Ethiopian Shiro Wat
description: Shiro, a smooth, spiced chickpea flour stew, is one of Ethiopia's most common everyday dishes, real technique whisking the flour into liquid gradually to avoid lumps.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion in the oil, 6-7 minutes, then add the garlic and berbere, cooking 1 minute.
Whisk the chickpea flour with 1.5 cups water until completely smooth, then stir into the pot gradually.
Simmer, stirring often to prevent lumps, 10-12 minutes, until thickened and smooth.

name: Ethiopian Gomen
description: Gomen, collard greens simmered simply with garlic and ginger, is a genuine Ethiopian staple side shared with Ethiopia's neighbors, real technique keeping the greens tender but not mushy by not over-simmering once they wilt.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion, garlic, and ginger in the oil, 3-4 minutes, until fragrant.
Add the collard greens and a splash of water, and simmer 15-18 minutes until just tender - pull it off the heat as soon as the greens wilt fully, so they don't turn mushy.

name: Ethiopian Kitfo
description: Kitfo, real Ethiopian minced beef seasoned with mitmita and warm niter kibbeh, is traditionally served raw or very lightly warmed - this version cooks it through as a safer home approximation, though it changes the dish's real character.
steps_detailed: Cook the beef in the ghee over medium heat, breaking it up finely, 6-7 minutes, until just cooked through.
Stir in the chili powder and cardamom, echoing the warmth of real mitmita spice.

name: Ethiopian Atkilt Wat
description: Atkilt wat, cabbage, carrot, and potato cooked with real turmeric, a common Ethiopian vegetable side, mild in contrast to the berbere-forward stews.
steps_detailed: Cook the potato and carrot in the oil with the turmeric, 8-9 minutes.
Add the cabbage and a splash of water, and simmer 12-15 minutes until everything is tender.

name: Ethiopian Sega Wat
description: Sega wat, beef stewed in the same real dry-onion, berbere, and niter kibbeh technique as doro wat, is a beloved everyday version without the egg, real technique letting the onions cook completely dry and unattended before adding any fat.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion alone in a dry pot, no oil, 20-22 minutes, stirring often, until deeply caramelized.
Add the ghee, garlic, and ginger, cooking 2 minutes, then stir in the berbere and cook 2 minutes more until fragrant.
Add the beef and a splash of water, and simmer 30-35 minutes until tender.

name: Ethiopian Ayib
description: Ayib, a mild, crumbly fresh cheese similar to a dry cottage cheese, is a genuine Ethiopian staple often served alongside spicy stews to cool the palate - real ayib is traditionally made by simply letting soured milk separate, then draining the curds, with no rennet or culture needed.
steps_detailed: Drain the cottage cheese well in a fine sieve for a few minutes, pressing gently to remove excess liquid, until it reaches a dry, crumbly texture.
Toss with the chopped mint and serve alongside spicy stews to cool the palate between bites.

name: Ethiopian Timatim Salata
description: Timatim salata, a simple, bright tomato and onion salad, is a common Ethiopian accompaniment served alongside injera and richer stews, real versions letting the onion sit briefly in the lemon juice first to mellow its raw bite.
steps_detailed: Toss the onion with the lemon juice and let sit 5 minutes to mellow its sharpness.
Add the tomatoes, jalapeño, and olive oil, and toss together.

name: Ethiopian Beef Stew
description: A simple, hearty beef and vegetable stew, common Ethiopian home cooking outside the berbere-forward wats, real technique browning the beef in real batches so it sears properly rather than steaming from overcrowding the pan.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef in batches if needed, 8-9 minutes total, so each piece sears rather than steams.
Add the onion and cook 3-4 minutes.
Add the carrot, potato, and tomatoes, and simmer 30-35 minutes until everything is tender.

name: Ethiopian Niter Kibbeh
description: Niter kibbeh, Ethiopian spiced clarified butter, is the real aromatic foundation underlying countless Ethiopian dishes - real versions simmer whole spices directly in the melting butter, infusing it, rather than just stirring ground spice into plain butter afterward.
steps_detailed: Gently warm the ghee with the ginger, turmeric, garlic, and cardamom for 4-5 minutes to infuse the flavors directly into the fat.
Strain out the solids before using.

name: Ethiopian Berbere-Style Spice Blend
description: Berbere, Ethiopia's signature and most essential spice blend, real versions containing a dozen or more spices including fenugreek and cardamom - this simplified version captures the warm, layered heat with what's realistically available.
steps_detailed: Toast the chili powder and paprika briefly in a dry pan, 30 seconds, just until fragrant, to wake up their flavor.
Mix in the remaining spices and store in an airtight container.

name: Ethiopian Awaze Sauce
description: Awaze, a fiery berbere-based dipping sauce, is a common Ethiopian condiment for grilled meat, real versions often loosened with a little of the meat's own cooking liquid or wine rather than oil alone.
steps_detailed: Mix the berbere with the olive oil, garlic, and lemon juice into a thick, spoonable paste.
Let sit 10 minutes before serving so the garlic mellows slightly.
